newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court dismisses appeal in lesbian officer case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court dismisses appeal in lesbian officer case.

text.p: A federal appeals court Monday dismissed a U.S. government appeal of a ruling that its old policy on gays in the military was unconstitutional, saying the case had been overtaken by events.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the appeal in the case of Col. Margarethe Cammermeyer was moot because the regulation under which she was discharged for lesbianism had been rescinded and she had been reinstated.
Cammermeyer, 54, is a highly decorated nurse who won the Bronze Star for distinguished service in Vietnam.

While serving in the Washington State National Guard, Cammermeyer sought admission to the Army War College. During an interview to obtain "top secret" security clearance, she was asked about her sexual orientation.
According to the court record, she replied that she was a lesbian and that lesbianism was an emotional orientation she had that did not imply sexual activity.
Cammermeyer was discharged from the National Guard in 1992 under a regulation then in force that a statement of homosexuality was grounds for separation from the military.

Cammermeyer sued to challenge her discharge, saying that the regulation violated her constitutional rights. U.S. District Judge Thomas Zilly of Seattle declared her discharge and the army regulation unconstitutional and ordered her reinstated in 1994.

Pending appeal, Cammermeyer was reinstated. The Clinton administration then replaced the old regulation on homosexuality with the new "don't ask, don't tell" policy, which bans homosexual conduct rather than orientation.

Defence Secretary William Perry and other defendants appealed Zilly's decision, saying the judge should not have ruled on the constitutionality of the old regulation or of the discharge and asking for that part of his ruling to be annulled.
The appeals court said that, since the authorities had reinstated Cammermeyer and rescinded the regulation under which she had been discharged, it could not help anyone by reviewing the case.

"Federal courts do not have the power to decide questions that cannot affect the rights of the litigants in the case before them. Because federal courts may resolve only real and substantial controversies...the case is moot," it said.
The appeals court did however send the case back to Zilly to decide whether to annul his previous finding of unconstitutionality.
Mary Newcombe, a lawyer for Cammermeyer, said her client was disappointed that the appeals court did not affirm the lower court decision.
